title: SVDQuant-GPTQ for Wan2.2 in five minutes

stops.title: The question
stops.text: This paper is the closest cousin of the LTX-2.3 project. The authors take Wan 2.2, an image to video diffusion transformer with two experts of about fourteen billion parameters each, and ask whether it can run with four bit weights and four bit activations, called W four A four, without any retraining. The model is similar in scale to LTX-2.3, and the method is pure post-training quantization. So listen for which parts transfer to NNCF, and which parts only make sense on an NVIDIA GPU.

stops.title: Three tools, one layer
stops.text: Here is the whole idea in one picture. Nothing in it is new on its own. The paper stacks three tools already covered in this atlas onto every linear layer. Offline, each weight is smoothed and split into a sixteen bit low-rank part plus a four bit residual, and that residual is rounded with GPTQ. Then a clipping ratio is searched for every expert, layer and timestep bin. At inference, the only extra work is a table lookup keyed by the current step.

stops.title: Problem one: outliers
stops.text: Why is four bit so hard? Four bits give only sixteen levels. If a single channel carries a huge value, the grid has to stretch to cover it, and all the normal values end up sharing two or three codes. That is the same outlier story told in SmoothQuant and SVDQuant. The smoothing step and the low-rank branch exist to take those extreme directions out of the part that gets rounded.

stops.title: Problem two: the range drifts
stops.text: The second problem is specific to diffusion. The activation range is wide in the early, noisy steps and much narrower in the late ones. One global clipping threshold therefore over-clips the early steps and wastes levels on the late ones. The staircase in this drawing is the paper's answer: a separate threshold for each timestep bin. And because Wan has two experts, with the low-noise expert more fragile, the bins are searched separately for each expert.

stops.title: The recipe step by step
stops.text: Now the method in order. First, smooth each layer so the activation outliers move into the weight. Second, split the weight with a singular value decomposition, keep the low-rank part in high precision, and round the residual to four bits with GPTQ, using calibration data instead of plain rounding. Third, cut the denoising trajectory into a few bins, and for each layer and bin try a handful of clip ratios, keeping the one whose output is closest to BF16. It is a grid search, not training.

stops.title: Where the error lives
stops.text: This heatmap is the part most worth remembering. It shows the reconstruction error of every linear module type across the forty blocks. Notice that the error depends on the kind of module, not on which block it sits in. The attention output projection and the feed-forward down projection are the worst in both experts, while query, key and cross-attention output are robust. That is a sensitivity map that can be tested directly on LTX-2.3.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: Here is what each ingredient buys. Plain round to nearest gives a VBench average of 0.733. Adding SVDQuant lifts it to 0.783, GPTQ to 0.793, and timestep clipping to 0.799, against 0.806 for full precision. Careful: the axis is truncated, so the bars exaggerate. SVDQuant does most of the rescue, and the timestep search adds the least, which fits the fact that almost every layer picks a ratio of 0.8 anyway.

stops.title: The catch: no speed-up
stops.text: And here is the cost that matters. Memory drops by about 59 percent, from roughly 64 gigabytes to 26. But each video takes about 1.8 times longer, 955 seconds instead of 521. The four bit values are unpacked in Python right before a normal BF16 matrix multiply, because there was no fused FP4 kernel. Weight-only W four A sixteen already gets almost all the memory gain at nearly full speed. Fewer bits only mean faster inference when the kernels exist.

stops.title: What the thesis takes from it
stops.text: So the thesis takes the sensitivity map, not the W four A four recipe. When the authors kept just those two sensitive module types in higher precision, quality came back to 0.803. The first NNCF experiment writes itself: int4 weights everywhere, with the attention output and feed-forward down projections kept at int8, calibrated on inputs from every timestep. Then measure real memory and time per step. Next, FlashAttention-2 turns to that speed question, making attention itself fast.
